passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of different lighting conditions on cognitive task performance in a controlled laboratory setting. The experiment involved 120 adult participants randomly assigned to one of four lighting conditions: (1) standard office lighting (400 lux), (2) dimmed lighting (200 lux), (3) bright LED lighting (800 lux), and (4) natural daylight (variable lux). Each participant completed a 30‑minute working memory task while their reaction times and accuracy were recorded. The researchers hypothesized that brighter lighting would improve task performance, while dim lighting would impair it. Data were collected over a two‑week period, and participants were blinded to the study’s purpose to reduce expectancy effects. The study also measured subjective mood ratings after each session to assess potential confounding variables. Statistical analysis involved ANOVA to compare mean reaction times across conditions, followed by post‑hoc Tukey tests to identify specific group differences. The results indicated a significant main effect of lighting on reaction time (p < .01), with the bright LED condition yielding the fastest responses and the dimmed condition the slowest. Accuracy rates did not differ significantly across conditions, suggesting that lighting primarily affected speed rather than correctness.
stem: Which lighting condition produced the fastest average reaction time?
explanation: The table shows the mean response time for each condition. The Bright LED lighting condition has the lowest mean (590 ms), indicating the fastest reaction time.
trap: Assuming the highest-lux condition cannot be the fastest, or misreading the table and choosing standard office lighting (650 ms) instead of the lowest mean, 590 ms.

explanation: The independent variable is the factor that the researchers manipulate; in this case, the lighting condition.
trap: Students sometimes confuse the dependent variable (reaction time) with the independent variable.

stem: What is the percent increase in mean reaction time from the bright LED condition to the dimmed condition?
explanation: Correct: A) Percent increase = (720 - 590)/590 x 100 = 22.0%, using the bright LED value as the starting point. Why the others are wrong: B) 15.5% does not follow from these values. C) 18.1% divides the 130 ms difference by 720, the wrong denominator. D) 21.3% does not follow from these values.
trap: Dividing the 130 ms increase by the dimmed value (720) instead of the bright LED reference (590) gives 18.1%, a common denominator error.

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data presented?

options.A: Bright LED lighting leads to faster reaction times than dimmed lighting.
options.B: Accuracy rates did not differ significantly across lighting conditions.
options.C: Participants were randomly assigned to lighting conditions.
options.D: Natural daylight produced the slowest reaction times.

explanation: Correct: D) Natural daylight had a mean of 630 ms; dimmed lighting (720 ms) was the slowest. Why the others are wrong: A) Bright LED (590 ms) was faster than dimmed (720 ms), so this is supported. B) The passage states accuracy did not differ significantly across conditions. C) The passage states participants were randomly assigned to one of four conditions.
trap: Assuming the variable-lux daylight condition must be the slowest because of its variability; its mean (630 ms) was second fastest, and dimmed lighting (720 ms) was slowest.

stem: How could the findings of this study be applied to improve workplace productivity?

options.A: Install dimmed lighting to reduce employee fatigue.
options.B: Use bright LED lighting in task‑intensive areas to speed up cognitive performance.
options.C: Eliminate all artificial lighting in favor of natural daylight.
options.D: Maintain standard office lighting to preserve consistency.

explanation: The study shows that bright LED lighting (800 lux) led to the fastest reaction times, implying that brighter lighting can enhance speed of cognitive tasks, which is beneficial for productivity in task‑intensive settings.
trap: Assuming natural daylight must be best because it is natural; its mean (630 ms) was slower than bright LED (590 ms), so the data favor bright LED for speed.
